query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coatings, the wear resistance and microscopic deformation during high-temperature sliding are governed primarily by the stability and distribution of nanoscale oxide phases formed at the surface; increasing the copper content in the alloy reduces the stability of protective oxide films, leading to increased wear and localized plastic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating (nominal equiatomic composition) deposited as a thin layer on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Increase the copper content in the alloy coating (e.g., from equiatomic to Cu-rich composition).
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests at temperatures above 600°C in air, with constant load and sliding speed.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale oxide phases (e.g., Cr2O3, NiO) formed at the coating surface during high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: Copper enrichment disrupts the formation and continuity of stable protective oxides, resulting in less effective surface passivation, increased oxidation, and enhanced localized plasticity during sliding.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline equiatomic coating, the Cu-rich coating will exhibit higher wear rates and more pronounced microscopic deformation (e.g., deeper grooves, more plastic flow) under high-temperature sliding.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu coating under identical test conditions.
generation.boundary: Predictions are expected to hold for sliding wear tests above 600°C in air; at lower temperatures or in inert atmospheres, the effect may be diminished.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of wear rate increase and deformation is uncertain due to lack of quantitative prior evidence; the role of substrate-coating adhesion and possible interdiffusion is not fully addressed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare FeNiCrCoCu coatings with equiatomic and Cu-rich compositions on identical substrates. Conduct sliding wear tests at >600°C in air, measure wear rate and analyze surface morphology and oxide phase distribution using SEM and XRD.
measurements: Wear rate (volume loss per unit distance)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu-rich coating does not show significantly higher wear rate and more pronounced microscopic deformation compared to the equiatomic coating, or if stable protective oxides persist in both cases, the hypothesis is falsified.
